summary.text: Writing the coefficient as \(3^n\prod_{j<n}(9j+2)(9j+4)(9j+7)\big/\big((n!)^2\prod_{j<n}(3j+1)\big)\), the proof shows that the denominator’s valuation is at most the numerator’s at every prime.  For \(p\ne3\), valuations are expressed as counts of solutions modulo each \(p^i\), and a six-case analysis of \(p^i\bmod 9\), together with monotonicity in the least residue representative, gives the required count inequality; for \(p=3\), the explicit factor \(3^n\) suffices because \(2v_3(n!)\le n\) and all other factors are prime to \(3\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(x)={}_3F_2\!\left(\frac29,\frac49,\frac79;\frac13,1;729x\right)
     =\sum_{n\ge 0}a(n)x^n.
\]
We prove that every coefficient \(a(n)\) is an integer.

Recall that the coefficient of \(z^n\) in
\({}_3F_2(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3;\beta_1,\beta_2;z)\) is
\[
\frac{(\alpha_1)_n(\alpha_2)_n(\alpha_3)_n}
     {(\beta_1)_n(\beta_2)_n}\frac1{n!},
\]
where \((u)_n=u(u+1)\cdots(u+n-1)\), with \((u)_0=1\). Since \((1)_n=n!\), we have
\[
a(n)=729^n\frac{(2/9)_n(4/9)_n(7/9)_n}{(1/3)_n(n!)^2}.
\]
Writing out the rising factorials gives
\[
(2/9)_n=9^{-n}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(9j+2),\qquad
(4/9)_n=9^{-n}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(9j+4),
\]
\[
(7/9)_n=9^{-n}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(9j+7),\qquad
(1/3)_n=3^{-n}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(3j+1).
\]
Because \(729=3^6\) and \(9^3=3^6\), the total scalar factor is
\(729^n3^n/9^{3n}=3^n\). Thus
\[
a(n)=\frac{N_n}{D_n},                                      \tag{1}
\]
where
\[
N_n=3^n\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(9j+2)(9j+4)(9j+7),
\qquad
D_n=(n!)^2\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(3j+1).                          \tag{2}
\]
Both are positive integers. It is therefore enough to prove
\[
D_n\mid N_n.                                                \tag{3}
\]
We will prove this by comparing the exponent of every prime in the two sides.

First we establish the counting inequality that drives the proof. For positive integers \(m,n\) and \(0\le a<m\), put
\[
C_{m,n}(a)=\#\{j:0\le j<n,\ j\equiv a\pmod m\}.
\]
If \(0\le a\le b<m\), then
\[
C_{m,n}(b)\le C_{m,n}(a).                                  \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, every nonnegative integer congruent to \(b\) modulo \(m\) has the form \(b+km\). Sending it to \(a+km\) preserves distinctness and, since \(a\le b\), sends every such integer below \(n\) to an integer below \(n\). This is an injection from the set counted by \(C_{m,n}(b)\) into that counted by \(C_{m,n}(a)\).

Suppose now that \(3\nmid m\). Then both \(3\) and \(9\) are invertible modulo \(m\). Consequently each of
\[
9j+2\equiv0,\quad 9j+4\equiv0,\quad 9j+7\equiv0,
\quad 3j+1\equiv0\pmod m                                  \tag{5}
\]
has exactly one residue-class solution modulo \(m\). Denote their representatives in \([0,m-1]\) by \(a_2,a_4,a_7,a_3\), respectively. Also, the solution of \(j+1\equiv0\pmod m\) is \(m-1\). Therefore
\[
\#\{0\le j<n:m\mid 9j+r\}=C_{m,n}(a_r)\quad(r=2,4,7),
\]
\[
\#\{0\le j<n:m\mid 3j+1\}=C_{m,n}(a_3),
\qquad
\#\{0\le j<n:m\mid j+1\}=C_{m,n}(m-1).                   \tag{6}
\]

We now give explicit representatives and compare them. Since \(3\nmid m\), its residue modulo \(9\) is one of \(1,2,4,5,7,8\). In the following table, each displayed quotient is an integer, lies between \(0\) and \(m-1\), and solves the corresponding congruence in (5):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
 m\bmod 9&a_2&a_4&a_7&a_3&\text{comparison used}\\ \hline
1&(2m-2)/9&(4m-4)/9&(7m-7)/9&(m-1)/3&a_2\le a_3\\
2&(m-2)/9&(2m-4)/9&(8m-7)/9&(2m-1)/3&a_2\le a_3\\
4&(5m-2)/9&(m-4)/9&(4m-7)/9&(m-1)/3&a_4\le a_3\\
5&(4m-2)/9&(8m-4)/9&(5m-7)/9&(2m-1)/3&a_2\le a_3\\
7&(8m-2)/9&(7m-4)/9&(m-7)/9&(m-1)/3&a_7\le a_3\\
8&(7m-2)/9&(5m-4)/9&(2m-7)/9&(2m-1)/3&a_7\le a_3.
\end{array}                                                  \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, all assertions in the table follow directly by writing \(m=9q+r\). For example, in the row \(r=4\),
\[
a_2=5q+2,\quad a_4=q,\quad a_7=4q+1,\quad a_3=3q+1.
\]
Then
\(9a_2+2=5m\), \(9a_4+4=m\), \(9a_7+7=4m\), and
\(3a_3+1=m\), and \(a_4\le a_3\). The other five rows work identically: multiplication by \(9\) or \(3\) shows that the displayed value solves the stated congruence, and substitution \(m=9q+r\) proves the range and comparison assertions. More explicitly, the multiples of \(m\) obtained from \(9a_2+2,9a_4+4,9a_7+7,3a_3+1\) in the six rows are respectively
\[
(2,4,7,1),\ (1,2,8,2),\ (5,1,4,1),\ (4,8,5,2),\ (8,7,1,1),\ (7,5,2,2).
\]
This also confirms all four congruences in every row.

Let
\[
A=C_{m,n}(m-1),\quad B=C_{m,n}(a_3),\quad
X=C_{m,n}(a_2),\quad Y=C_{m,n}(a_4),\quad Z=C_{m,n}(a_7).
\]
Because each \(a_2,a_4,a_7\le m-1\), monotonicity (4) gives
\[
A\le X,\qquad A\le Y,\qquad A\le Z.                        \tag{8}
\]
The last column of (7) says that at least one of \(a_2,a_4,a_7\) is at most \(a_3\). Applying (4) once more shows that the corresponding one of \(X,Y,Z\) is at least \(B\). Assign \(B\) to that term and \(A\) to each of the other two terms. We obtain
\[
2A+B\le X+Y+Z.
\]
Using (6), this is the following fundamental inequality, valid for every positive \(m\) not divisible by \(3\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&2\#\{0\le j<n:m\mid j+1\}
 +\#\{0\le j<n:m\mid3j+1\}\\
&\qquad\le
 \#\{0\le j<n:m\mid9j+2\}
 +\#\{0\le j<n:m\mid9j+4\}
 +\#\{0\le j<n:m\mid9j+7\}.
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{9}
\]

We apply (9) to prime powers. For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(t)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(t\). We use the elementary identity
\[
v_p(t)=\sum_{i\ge1}\mathbf 1_{p^i\mid t}.                  \tag{10}
\]
The sum is finite because \(p^i>t\) for sufficiently large \(i\). Summing (10) over a finite family of positive integers and interchanging the two finite sums gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}v_p(g(j))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\#\{0\le j<n:p^i\mid g(j)\}.                \tag{11}
\]
In particular, since \(n!=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(j+1)\),
\[
v_p(n!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\#\{0\le j<n:p^i\mid j+1\}.        \tag{12}
\]

Let \(p\ne3\) be prime. For every \(i\ge1\), the modulus \(m=p^i\) is positive and is not divisible by \(3\). Applying (9) with \(m=p^i\), and then summing over all \(i\ge1\), equations (11) and (12) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
2v_p(n!)+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}v_p(3j+1)
&\le \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}v_p(9j+2)
 +\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}v_p(9j+4)\\
&\qquad+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}v_p(9j+7).                         \tag{13}
\end{aligned}
\]
All sums are finite, so there is no convergence issue. By (2), and because \(v_p(3)=0\) for \(p\ne3\), the left side of (13) is exactly \(v_p(D_n)\), while the right side is exactly \(v_p(N_n)\). Hence
\[
v_p(D_n)\le v_p(N_n)\qquad(p\ne3).                       \tag{14}
\]

It remains to treat \(p=3\). None of \(3j+1\), \(9j+2\), \(9j+4\), or \(9j+7\) is divisible by \(3\). Therefore (2) gives
\[
v_3(D_n)=2v_3(n!),\qquad v_3(N_n)=n.                       \tag{15}
\]
By Legendre’s formula,
\[
v_3(n!)=\sum_{k\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{3^k}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently
\[
v_3(n!)\le \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{n}{3^k}=\frac n2,
\]
and hence, since the valuation is an integer,
\[
2v_3(n!)\le n.                                              \tag{16}
\]
Combining (15) and (16) gives
\[
v_3(D_n)\le v_3(N_n).                                     \tag{17}
\]

Thus \(v_p(D_n)\le v_p(N_n)\) for every prime \(p\). The prime-factorization criterion for divisibility now implies \(D_n\mid N_n\), proving (3). Equation (1) therefore expresses \(a(n)\) as the quotient of two positive integers with the denominator dividing the numerator, so \(a(n)\in\mathbb Z\).

The argument also includes \(n=0\): all products are empty, \(N_0=D_0=1\), and \(a(0)=1\). Hence every coefficient of
\({}_3F_2(2/9,4/9,7/9;1/3,1;729x)\) is an integer.
